clue.text: Clue one composed about power and riches

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters are placed around the next piece
composed means put together afresh, so the letters of clue one are rearranged

parts.note: P is the standard abbreviation for power in physics

explanation.surface: A setter composes a clue about the theme of power and wealth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composed' rearranges CLUEONE into OULENCE, and 'about' puts that round P.
explanation.definitionFit: Opulence is great wealth or luxury, a synonym for riches.

clue.text: Deep water shelter put up around small port

indicators.note: around means the reversed shelter word surrounds the port abbreviation
in a down clue put up means the word is written upwards, read backwards

parts.note: a shed is a simple shelter
PT is a short form of port

explanation.surface: A shelter is erected near a little harbour by deep water.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'put up' means written upwards, so the shelter word reads backwards (giving DEHS), and 'around' wraps it round the port abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: The depths are the deepest parts of the sea, deep water.

clue.text: Driver of train having crossed lines

definitions.text: Driver of train having crossed lines

parts.words: Driver of train having crossed lines
parts.note: a mule is a crossbreed, so a train of hybrid animals in lines needs its driver

explanation.surface: A railway driver has gone through the signals onto the wrong track.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a locomotive; the train is a line of mules, animals bred from a cross of horse and donkey.
explanation.definitionFit: A muleteer is the person who drives a string of pack mules.

clue.text: Military show leaves a permanent impression on one

definitions.meaning: a display of marching and music by troops, as at Edinburgh

definitions.text: leaves a permanent impression on one
definitions.meaning: an inked design pricked permanently into the skin

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both an evening military display and an inked skin design.

clue.text: Metal detector

definitions.meaning: slang for a police officer, who detects crime

explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the reddish element and, as slang, a police officer.

clue.text: Stop these jokes

definitions.meaning: gaps or fissures that one stops up with filler

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both fissures one fills and quips, as in cracking jokes.

clue.text: Compassionate chap involved in outcry

indicators.note: involved in means one word is wrapped up inside the other

parts.note: hue as in hue and cry, a public outcry
a chap is a man

explanation.surface: A kind-hearted fellow gets caught up in a public protest.
explanation.walkthrough: HUE is the outcry of 'hue and cry'.
explanation.definitionFit: Humane means showing kindness and compassion.

clue.text: Lure damaged net on the rocks

indicators.note: damaged means the letters of net are knocked out of order

parts.note: a drink on the rocks is served over ice

explanation.surface: A fishing net, torn on rocks, is used as bait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damaged' turns NET into ENT; 'on the rocks' is the bar phrase for served with ice.
explanation.definitionFit: To entice is to tempt or attract, a synonym for lure.

clue.text: Mixed metaphors in Molière play

indicators.note: mixed means the letters of metaphors in are jumbled

explanation.surface: A critic complains of mixed metaphors in a play by Molière.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mixed' looks like part of the phrase mixed metaphors, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Le Misanthrope is a 1666 comedy by the French playwright Molière.

clue.text: Play for the village

definitions.meaning: Shakespeare's tragedy of the Danish prince

explanation.definitionFit: The word is both Shakespeare's Danish tragedy and a term for a small settlement.

clue.text: In which the innocent align themselves with the guilty

definitions.text: In which the innocent align themselves with the guilty

parts.words: In which the innocent align themselves with the guilty
parts.note: at a police line-up innocent volunteers literally stand in a row beside the suspect

explanation.surface: Blameless people side morally with wrongdoers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'align themselves with' reads as taking sides; here it means standing in a line beside the suspect.
explanation.definitionFit: A police line-up places innocent people in a row with a suspect for a witness to pick out.

clue.text: The depth of beauty?

parts.note: from the saying that beauty is only so deep, as far as the outer covering

explanation.surface: A philosophical question about how deep beauty goes.
explanation.walkthrough: It plays on the proverb that beauty is only skin-deep.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says beauty goes no deeper than the body's outer covering.

clue.text: Boards train — a form of transport once regularly used

definitions.text: a form of transport once regularly used

parts.note: the boards are the theatre stage
to train someone is to coach them

explanation.surface: Someone gets on a train, a form of transport once in common use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boards' looks like a verb for getting on; it is the theatre's boards.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse-drawn coach running between stages was a regular means of travel before railways.

clue.text: Break alternative arrangements

indicators.note: arrangements means the letters of alternative are set in a new order

explanation.surface: A notice says that other arrangements will be made because of a break.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket the afternoon pause for refreshment is a break in play.

clue.text: Risk including a kind of measure

indicators.note: including means the first word holds the next inside it

parts.note: to imperil is to put at risk

explanation.surface: A gamble that involves some sort of measure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'including' puts A inside IMPERIL.
explanation.definitionFit: The imperial system of pints, feet and pounds is a set of units of measurement.

clue.text: Openings for upper members

parts.note: the upper limbs are arms, and garments have gaps for them

explanation.surface: Vacancies are advertised for senior members of a club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upper members' suggests senior people; it means the upper limbs.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the holes in a garment through which the arms go.

clue.text: Regions about to receive handouts

parts.note: re means about, concerning
alms are charitable handouts

explanation.surface: Areas are about to be given charity.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'about to receive' as soon to get; in fact 'about' is the first piece and 'to receive' just links it to the charity that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Realms are kingdoms or domains, so regions.

clue.text: See 10
Fresh meat and drink provide morale

indicators.note: fresh means the letters of meat are made anew

parts.note: a spirit is a strong drink such as gin

explanation.surface: Food and drink are laid on to keep up morale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fresh' rearranges MEAT into TEAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Group morale is the sense of loyalty and enthusiasm members share.

clue.text: Plan spread out of African capital

parts.note: a map is a plan of an area

indicators.note: spread means the letters of out are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A map spread out showing an African capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spread' rearranges OUT into UTO.
explanation.definitionFit: Maputo is the capital city of Mozambique, in Africa.

clue.text: Light meal for Indian pet at home

parts.note: a pet is a fit of sulking, as is a tiff, a petty quarrel
in means at home

explanation.surface: Food for an Indian pet kept in the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pet' looks like an animal; it is an old word for a sulk, as in 'in a pet'.
explanation.definitionFit: In India, especially under British rule, this was a light lunch or snack.

clue.text: It should contain enough water to go round

definitions.text: It should contain enough water to go round

parts.words: It should contain enough water to go round
parts.note: a defensive ditch full of water encircles a castle

explanation.surface: A host makes sure there is enough water for everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go round' seems to mean be shared out; it means encircle.
explanation.definitionFit: A castle's water-filled ditch runs all the way round it.

clue.text: Applaud the actor's role — on reflection, it's rubbish

parts.note: to clap is to applaud

indicators.note: on reflection means the role word is mirrored, read backwards

parts.note: an actor's role is a part

explanation.surface: A critic first applauds the actor, then thinks better of it and calls it rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on reflection' turns PART into TRAP.
explanation.definitionFit: Claptrap is pretentious nonsense, a synonym for rubbish.

clue.text: Free-for-all in kind of dance in Cornwall

indicators.note: free means the letters of for all are let loose into a new order

explanation.surface: A chaotic free-for-all breaks out at a Cornish dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free-for-all' looks like one word for a brawl; split it, and 'Free' rearranges FORALL.
explanation.definitionFit: The Helston Furry Dance, held in Cornwall every May, is also called the Floral Dance.

clue.text: Took a seat on returning vehicle — one way to get home?

parts.note: sat means took a seat

indicators.note: returning means the vehicle word is read backwards

parts.note: a van is a vehicle

explanation.surface: Someone sits down in a van heading back, one way of getting home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns VAN into NAV.
explanation.definitionFit: A satellite navigation device guides a driver to a destination, such as home.

clue.text: It had row upon row of rowers

definitions.text: It had row upon row of rowers

parts.words: It had row upon row of rowers
parts.note: an ancient galley with two banks of oars stacked one above the other

explanation.surface: Something had many lines of oarsmen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row upon row' sounds like many rows; here it is exactly two tiers, one upon the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A bireme was an ancient warship with two banks of oars.
